name: Force (F = ma)
description: Applies Newton's second law, F=mass×acceleration, to find the net force on an object in newtons from its mass in kg and acceleration in m/s².
notes: This gives the net (resultant) force. Use SI units (kg, m/s²) so the result is in newtons; force acts in the direction of acceleration.

name: Kinetic energy
description: Computes translational kinetic energy as ½×mass×velocity², giving the energy of motion in joules from mass in kg and speed in m/s.
notes: Velocity is squared, so doubling speed quadruples the energy. Use m/s for velocity; the result assumes non-relativistic (everyday) speeds.

name: Potential energy
description: Computes gravitational potential energy as mass×g×height, the energy stored by lifting a mass to a given height, in joules.
notes: Height is measured from your chosen reference level. Near Earth's surface g≈9.81 m/s²; the value is only accurate for modest heights.

name: Pressure (P = F/A)
description: Computes pressure as force÷area, the force distributed per unit area, in pascals from force in newtons and area in m².
notes: Force must act perpendicular to the surface. Area must be nonzero; 1 pascal equals 1 N/m², so use m² to get pascals.

name: Wave speed (v = fλ)
description: Computes wave speed as frequency×wavelength, giving how fast a wave propagates in m/s from its frequency in hertz and wavelength in metres.
notes: Applies to any periodic wave in a uniform medium. Frequency in Hz and wavelength in m give speed in m/s; keep units consistent.

name: Newton's second law (F=ma)
description: Applies Newton's second law F=m×a to find the net force in newtons from mass in kg and acceleration in m/s². Force and acceleration point in the same direction.
notes: Gives the net force producing the acceleration. Use SI units (kg and m/s²) for a result in newtons; this describes the resultant of all forces.

name: Weight (W=mg)
description: Computes the weight (gravitational force) on a mass as m×g, in newtons from mass in kg and gravitational acceleration in m/s².
notes: Weight is a force in newtons, distinct from mass in kg. Near Earth's surface g≈9.81 m/s²; on other bodies use their local g.

name: Final velocity (v = u + at)
description: Computes the final velocity under constant acceleration as u+a×t, from initial velocity u, acceleration a and elapsed time t. It is a standard equation of motion.
notes: Valid only for constant (uniform) acceleration. Use consistent signs: a negative acceleration (deceleration) reduces the velocity over time.

name: Displacement (s = ut + ½at²)
description: Computes displacement under constant acceleration as u×t+½×a×t², the distance travelled from initial velocity u over time t while accelerating at a.
notes: Valid only for constant acceleration. The result is displacement (net position change) along the direction of motion, which can be negative.

name: Velocity from displacement (v = √(u²+2as))
description: Computes the final speed after a displacement s under constant acceleration, using √(u²+2×a×s), from initial velocity u. This equation of motion contains no time term.
notes: Valid only for constant acceleration. If u²+2as is negative the motion cannot reach that displacement and the square root has no real value.

name: Average velocity ((u+v)/2)
description: Computes average velocity as the mean of initial and final velocity, (u+v)÷2. This shortcut holds only when acceleration is constant.
notes: Valid only for uniform acceleration, where velocity changes linearly with time. It does not apply when acceleration varies during the interval.

name: Free fall distance (h = ½gt²)
description: Computes the distance fallen from rest under gravity as ½×g×t², from gravitational acceleration g and fall time t. The result is the drop height in metres.
notes: Assumes the object starts from rest with no air resistance. Real falls with drag fall shorter than this ideal value, especially over long times.

name: Free fall velocity (v = gt)
description: Computes the speed of an object falling from rest under gravity after a given time, as the product of gravitational acceleration g and elapsed time t. The result is the instantaneous speed in metres per second.
notes: Assumes the object starts from rest and air resistance is negligible; near Earth's surface g is about 9.81 m/s². Time must be in seconds, giving speed in m/s.

name: Projectile range
description: Gives the horizontal distance a projectile travels over level ground, from its launch speed v and launch angle theta, using v² sin(2θ)/g. The result is the range in metres.
notes: The angle theta must be in radians and air resistance is ignored. Launch and landing heights are assumed equal; maximum range occurs at 45 degrees (about 0.785 rad).

name: Projectile maximum height
description: Computes the peak height a projectile reaches above its launch point, from the vertical component of its launch velocity, using (v sinθ)²/(2g). The result is the maximum height in metres.
notes: The angle theta must be in radians and air resistance is neglected. Only the vertical velocity component contributes; height is measured relative to the launch point.

name: Projectile time of flight
description: Gives the total time a projectile stays in the air over level ground, from its launch speed and angle, using 2v sinθ/g. The result is the flight time in seconds.
notes: The angle theta must be in radians and air resistance is ignored. Assumes launch and landing at the same height; this is twice the time to reach peak height.

name: Centripetal acceleration (a = v²/r)
description: Computes the centripetal (inward) acceleration of an object moving in a circle of radius r at speed v, as v²/r. The result is the acceleration directed toward the centre, in m/s².
notes: Valid for uniform circular motion; the acceleration points toward the centre even at constant speed. Speed in m/s and radius in metres give m/s².

name: Centripetal force (F = mv²/r)
description: Computes the net inward force needed to keep a mass m moving in a circle of radius r at speed v, as mv²/r. The result is the centripetal force in newtons.
notes: This is the required net force toward the centre, not an extra force; it must be supplied by tension, gravity, friction, etc. Radius in metres and speed in m/s.

name: Angular velocity (ω = v/r)
description: Computes the angular velocity of an object in circular motion, relating its linear speed v and radius r as v/r. The result is how fast it sweeps angle, in radians per second.
notes: The output is in radians per second, not revolutions; multiply by r to recover linear speed. Valid for motion on a circle of constant radius.

name: Angular velocity from period (ω = 2π/T)
description: Computes the angular velocity of uniform circular or periodic motion from its period T, as 2π/T. The result is the angular velocity in radians per second.
notes: The period t is the time for one full revolution, in seconds; the constant tau equals 2π. A shorter period gives a larger angular velocity.

name: Centripetal acceleration (a = ω²r)
description: Computes the centripetal acceleration of an object in circular motion from its angular velocity w and radius r, as ω²r. The result is the inward acceleration in m/s².
notes: Angular velocity w must be in radians per second; this form is equivalent to v²/r since v = ωr. The acceleration points toward the centre.

name: Kinetic energy (½mv²)
description: Computes the translational kinetic energy of a mass m moving at speed v, as ½mv². The result is the energy of motion in joules.
notes: Energy scales with the square of speed, so doubling speed quadruples it. Mass in kilograms and speed in m/s give joules; this is translational energy only.

name: Gravitational potential energy (mgh)
description: Computes the gravitational potential energy of a mass m raised to height h in a uniform gravitational field, as mgh. The result is the stored energy in joules.
notes: Height h is measured from a chosen reference level, so only differences in energy are physically meaningful. Valid near Earth's surface where g is roughly constant.

name: Momentum (p = mv)
description: Computes the linear momentum of a mass m moving at velocity v, as the product mv. The result is the momentum in kilogram-metres per second.
notes: Momentum is a vector sharing the direction of the velocity; a sign on v indicates its direction. It is conserved in the absence of external forces.

name: Impulse (J = FΔt)
description: Computes the impulse delivered by a constant force f acting over a time interval t, as the product ft. The result equals the change in momentum, in newton-seconds.
notes: Assumes the force is constant over the interval; for varying forces use the average force. Impulse equals the change in momentum and has the same units as momentum.

name: Impulse–momentum (F = mΔv/Δt)
description: Computes the average force needed to change a mass m's velocity by dv over a time interval t, as m·dv/t. The result is the average force in newtons.
notes: This gives the average force over the interval, not the instantaneous peak. Velocity change dv is a signed quantity; a shorter time for the same change means a larger force.

name: Power (P = W/t)
description: Computes the average power as the work done divided by the time taken, work/t. The result is the rate of energy transfer in watts.
notes: This yields average power over the interval; work in joules and time in seconds give watts (one watt is one joule per second).

name: Power (P = Fv)
description: Computes the instantaneous mechanical power delivered by a force f acting on a body moving at velocity v, as the product fv. The result is the power in watts.
notes: Strictly valid when force and velocity are parallel; otherwise use their component along the motion. Force in newtons and velocity in m/s give watts.

name: Work (W = Fd cosθ)
description: Computes the work done by a constant force f over a displacement d, accounting for the angle theta between them, as f·d·cosθ. The result is the work in joules.
notes: The angle theta must be in radians; work is zero when force is perpendicular to displacement and negative when it opposes the motion.

name: Friction force (f = μN)
description: Computes the friction force between two surfaces as the product of the friction coefficient mu and the normal force n. The result is the friction force in newtons.
notes: The coefficient mu is dimensionless; use the static value for maximum friction before sliding and the kinetic value while sliding. Friction is independent of contact area here.

name: Force along incline (mg sinθ)
description: Computes the component of gravity acting down a frictionless incline on a mass m, as mg sinθ, where theta is the incline angle. The result is the accelerating force in newtons.
notes: The angle theta must be in radians, measured from the horizontal; this ignores friction. As the slope steepens toward 90 degrees this component approaches the full weight.

name: Normal force on incline (mg cosθ)
description: Computes the normal (perpendicular) force from an incline on a mass m, as mg cosθ, where theta is the incline angle. The result is the support force in newtons.
notes: The angle theta must be in radians, measured from the horizontal. On a flat surface (theta = 0) this equals the full weight; it decreases as the slope steepens.

name: Torque (τ = rF sinθ)
description: Computes the torque produced by a force f applied at a lever arm r, with angle theta between them, as r·f·sinθ. The result is the turning effect in newton-metres.
notes: The angle theta must be in radians; torque is maximal when force is perpendicular to the lever arm (theta = π/2) and zero when parallel.

name: Density (ρ = m/V)
description: Computes the density of a substance as its mass m divided by its volume v. The result is the mass per unit volume in kilograms per cubic metre.
notes: Mass in kilograms and volume in cubic metres give kg/m³; for reference, water is about 1000 kg/m³. Assumes the material is uniform throughout.

name: Hooke's law (F = kx)
description: Computes the restoring force of an ideal spring stretched or compressed by x, as the product of spring constant k and displacement x. The result is the force in newtons.
notes: Valid only within the spring's elastic limit where force is proportional to displacement; the actual restoring force opposes the displacement.

name: Elastic potential energy (½kx²)
description: Computes the elastic potential energy stored in a spring displaced by x from equilibrium, as ½kx². The result is the stored energy in joules.
notes: Valid within the elastic limit; energy grows with the square of displacement, so doubling x quadruples the stored energy. Displacement x is measured from equilibrium.

name: Mechanical advantage (MA = L/E)
description: Computes the mechanical advantage of a simple machine as the load force divided by the effort force. The result is a dimensionless factor showing how much the machine multiplies force.
notes: A value above 1 means the machine multiplies the applied force; the result is unitless as both inputs are forces. It reflects force ratio, not efficiency or energy.

name: Simple pendulum period (T = 2π√(L/g))
description: Computes the period of a simple pendulum of length l under gravity g, as 2π√(l/g). The result is the time for one complete swing, in seconds.
notes: Valid for small swing angles where the motion is approximately simple harmonic; the period is independent of the bob's mass. The constant tau equals 2π.

name: Mass-spring period (T = 2π√(m/k))
description: Computes the oscillation period of a mass m on a spring of stiffness k, as 2π√(m/k). The result is the time for one full oscillation, in seconds.
notes: Assumes an ideal, massless spring within its elastic limit and no damping; a stiffer spring or lighter mass gives a shorter period. The constant tau equals 2π.

name: Newton's law of gravitation
description: Computes the gravitational attraction between two masses m1 and m2 separated by distance r, as G·m1·m2/r². The result is the mutual force in newtons.
notes: The force weakens with the square of separation r, measured between centres of mass. Here g is the gravitational constant (about 6.674e-11 N·m²/kg²), not surface gravity.

name: Gravitational potential energy
description: Computes the gravitational potential energy of a mass m at height h in a uniform field of strength g, as mgh. The result is the stored energy in joules.
notes: Height h is relative to a chosen reference, so only energy differences matter. Valid near Earth's surface where g stays approximately constant.

name: Work done by a force
description: Computes the work done by a constant force f over a displacement d, with angle theta between them, as f·d·cosθ. The result is the energy transferred, in joules.
notes: The angle theta must be in radians; work is zero when the force is perpendicular to the displacement and negative when it opposes the motion.

name: Power (work over time)
description: Computes the average power as the work done w divided by the elapsed time t. The result is the rate of energy transfer in watts.
notes: This is average power over the interval; work in joules and time in seconds give watts (one watt equals one joule per second).

name: Elastic (spring) potential energy
description: Computes the elastic potential energy stored in a spring displaced by x from equilibrium, as ½kx². The result is the stored energy in joules.
notes: Valid within the elastic limit; the energy grows with the square of displacement x, which is measured from the spring's equilibrium position.

name: Hooke's law
description: Computes the restoring force of an ideal spring extended by x, as the product of spring constant k and extension x. The result is the force in newtons.
notes: Valid only within the elastic limit where force is proportional to extension; the real restoring force acts opposite to the displacement.

name: Gravitational field strength
description: Computes the gravitational field strength (acceleration due to gravity) at distance r from a body of mass m, as G·m/r². The result is the field strength in m/s².
notes: Distance r is measured from the body's centre and the field weakens with r². The constant gc is the gravitational constant (about 6.674e-11 N·m²/kg²).

name: Escape velocity
description: Computes the minimum speed needed to escape a body of mass m from radius r without further propulsion, as √(2Gm/r). The result is the escape velocity in metres per second.
notes: Ignores atmospheric drag and the body's rotation; it is independent of the escaping object's mass. Radius r is measured from the centre of the attracting body.

name: Orbital velocity
description: Computes the speed needed for a circular orbit at radius r around a central mass m, as √(Gm/r). The result is the orbital velocity in metres per second.
notes: Assumes a circular orbit and that the central mass dominates; orbital radius r is measured from its centre. Larger orbits correspond to slower orbital speeds.

name: Orbital period (Kepler)
description: Computes the period of a circular orbit at radius r around a central mass m, as 2π√(r³/(Gm)). The result is the time for one orbit, in seconds.
notes: This is Kepler's third law for a circular orbit; the period grows with r^1.5 and is independent of the orbiting body's mass. Radius r is from the centre.

name: Simple pendulum period
description: Computes the period of a simple pendulum of length l under gravity g, as 2π√(l/g). The result is the time for one complete swing, in seconds.
notes: Valid for small swing angles where the motion is approximately simple harmonic; the period does not depend on the bob's mass or amplitude.

name: Mass-spring period
description: Computes the oscillation period of a mass m on a spring of stiffness k, as 2π√(m/k). The result is the time for one full oscillation, in seconds.
notes: Assumes an ideal massless spring within its elastic limit and no damping; a stiffer spring or lighter mass shortens the period.

name: SHM displacement
description: Computes the displacement of a simple-harmonic oscillator at time t, as A cos(ωt), for amplitude a and angular frequency omega. The result is the position in metres.
notes: This form assumes the oscillator starts at maximum displacement (t = 0); omega is in radians per second and time t in seconds. The result ranges between +A and −A.

name: Momentum
description: Computes the linear momentum of a mass m moving at velocity v, as the product mv. The result is the momentum in kilogram-metres per second.
notes: Momentum is a vector with the direction of the velocity; the sign of v indicates direction. It is conserved when no external force acts.

name: Impulse
description: Computes the impulse delivered by a constant force f over a time interval t, as the product ft. The result equals the change in momentum, in newton-seconds.
notes: Assumes a constant force; for a varying force use its average value. Impulse equals the resulting change in momentum and shares its units.

name: Kinetic energy from momentum
description: Computes the kinetic energy of a mass m from its momentum p, as p²/(2m). The result is the energy of motion in joules.
notes: Equivalent to ½mv² since p = mv; useful when momentum is known instead of speed. Momentum in kg·m/s and mass in kilograms give joules.

name: Efficiency
description: Computes the efficiency of a machine or process as the useful power output divided by the total power input, expressed as a percentage. The result shows what fraction of input becomes useful output.
notes: The result is already scaled to a percentage, so no further multiplication is needed; it cannot exceed 100 percent for a real device. Both inputs must use the same units.

name: Work-energy theorem
description: Computes the net work done on a mass m from its change in kinetic energy, as ½m(vf² − vi²) between final and initial speeds. The result is the net work in joules.
notes: By the work-energy theorem this equals the total work by all forces; the result is negative when the object slows down. Speeds are in m/s.

name: Elastic collision final velocity
description: Computes the final velocity of body 1 after a one-dimensional elastic collision, from the two masses and their initial velocities, as ((m1−m2)u1 + 2m2·u2)/(m1+m2). The result is in metres per second.
notes: Valid only for perfectly elastic one-dimensional collisions, where both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved. Velocities are signed by direction.

name: Centre of mass (two bodies)
description: Computes the position of the centre of mass of two bodies from their masses and positions, as (m1·x1 + m2·x2)/(m1+m2). The result is the balance-point position in metres.
notes: Positions are measured along one axis from a common origin and may be negative. The centre of mass lies closer to the heavier body.

name: Power (force times velocity)
description: Computes the instantaneous mechanical power delivered by a force f to a body moving at velocity v, as the product fv. The result is the power in watts.
notes: Strictly valid when force and velocity are parallel; otherwise use the force component along the motion. Force in newtons and velocity in m/s give watts.

name: SHM maximum velocity
description: Computes the maximum speed of a simple-harmonic oscillator, reached at the equilibrium point, as the product of angular frequency omega and amplitude a. The result is in metres per second.
notes: Angular frequency omega must be in radians per second; this peak speed occurs as the oscillator passes through equilibrium, where displacement is zero.

name: SHM maximum acceleration
description: Computes the maximum acceleration of a simple-harmonic oscillator, reached at maximum displacement, as ω²a for angular frequency omega and amplitude a. The result is in m/s².
notes: Angular frequency omega must be in radians per second; this peak acceleration occurs at the extremes of motion and points back toward equilibrium.

name: Angular frequency from period
description: Converts an oscillation period into angular frequency, the rate of phase change in radians per second. It divides one full cycle of 2π radians by the period t, so a shorter period yields a proportionally larger angular frequency.
notes: The period must be in seconds so the result comes out in rad/s. Angular frequency ω differs from ordinary frequency f by a factor of 2π (ω = 2πf).

name: Gravitational potential energy (general)
description: Gives the gravitational potential energy of two point masses separated by distance r, taking the zero of energy at infinite separation. The result is negative because gravity is attractive, and it grows less negative as the masses move apart.
notes: This is the general form for any separation, not the near-surface mgh approximation. Use consistent SI units; r is the center-to-center distance, and the negative sign is physical, not an error.

name: Centripetal force
description: Computes the net inward force required to keep a mass m moving in a circle of radius r at speed v. The force scales with the square of the speed and inversely with the radius, always pointing toward the center of the circle.
notes: This is the required net force, not an extra force to add. Use tangential speed for v; doubling the speed quadruples the needed force.

name: Centripetal acceleration
description: Gives the center-directed acceleration of an object moving in a circle of radius r at speed v. It equals v squared divided by r, representing the constant change of velocity direction even when the speed is steady.
notes: Present even at constant speed, since only the direction of velocity changes. Use the instantaneous tangential speed for v and keep radius in meters.

name: Reduced mass
description: Calculates the reduced mass of a two-body system, an effective mass that lets the relative motion of two interacting masses be treated as a single-body problem. Its value is always smaller than either individual mass.
notes: Both masses must use the same unit. The reduced mass approaches the smaller mass when one body is far heavier than the other.

name: Weight
description: Computes the weight, the gravitational force on a mass m in a gravitational field of strength g. On Earth g is about 9.81 m/s squared, so a 70 kg mass weighs roughly 687 newtons.
notes: Weight is a force in newtons, not a mass in kilograms. The value of g varies with location and altitude and differs on other planets.

name: Torque
description: Calculates the torque produced by a force f applied at a lever arm r, where theta is the angle between the force and the arm. Torque is maximal at 90 degrees (sin = 1) and zero when the force is aligned with the arm.
notes: The angle theta must be in radians. Torque measures rotational effect; only the force component perpendicular to the lever arm contributes.

name: Angular momentum
description: Gives the angular momentum of a rotating rigid body as the product of its moment of inertia i and angular velocity omega. It is the rotational analog of linear momentum and is conserved when no external torque acts.
notes: Angular velocity should be in rad/s and moment of inertia about the same axis of rotation. This form applies to rigid-body rotation about a fixed axis.

name: Rotational kinetic energy
description: Computes the kinetic energy stored in a rotating body from its moment of inertia i and angular velocity omega. It mirrors the linear form (half m v squared), with the energy scaling as the square of the angular velocity.
notes: Angular velocity must be in rad/s, not revolutions per second. The moment of inertia depends on the axis and the mass distribution of the body.

name: Rotational power
description: Gives the mechanical power delivered by a torque acting on a body rotating at angular velocity omega. It is the rotational counterpart of force times velocity, so power rises with both the applied torque and the rotation rate.
notes: Angular velocity must be in rad/s to yield watts; convert from rpm if needed (multiply rpm by 2π/60). Valid for a torque applied about the rotation axis.

name: Total energy of SHM
description: Calculates the total mechanical energy of a simple harmonic oscillator such as a mass on a spring, from the spring constant k and amplitude a. This energy stays constant during the motion, continually shifting between kinetic and potential forms.
notes: Amplitude is the maximum displacement from equilibrium, in meters. The result assumes no damping or friction, so energy is conserved throughout each cycle.

name: Frequency from period
description: Converts a period into frequency by taking the reciprocal of the time for one full cycle. A period of 0.5 seconds corresponds to 2 cycles per second, or 2 hertz.
notes: The period must be in seconds so the frequency comes out in hertz. This gives ordinary frequency f, not angular frequency ω (which is 2π times larger).

name: Coefficient of restitution
description: Measures the elasticity of a collision as the ratio of the relative speed of separation after impact to the relative speed of approach before it. A value of 1 is a perfectly elastic collision, while 0 is perfectly inelastic.
notes: Use consistent signed velocities along the line of impact; the result is dimensionless and normally lies between 0 and 1. Order the velocity differences consistently to keep the sign positive.

name: Hydrostatic Pressure (ρgh)
description: Gives the gauge pressure exerted by a static column of fluid of density rho at depth h, in a gravitational field g. The pressure increases linearly with depth and does not depend on the shape or width of the container.
notes: This is the pressure due to the fluid alone; add surface (atmospheric) pressure to get absolute pressure. Keep density in kg/m³ and depth in meters.

name: Absolute Pressure at Depth
description: Computes the absolute pressure at depth h in a fluid by adding the hydrostatic pressure of the fluid column (rho g h) to the pressure P0 acting on the surface. Both the fluid weight and the overlying surface pressure contribute.
notes: P0 is often atmospheric pressure (about 101325 Pa). Use SI units throughout; the result is absolute pressure, not gauge pressure.

name: Buoyant Force (Archimedes)
description: Calculates the upward buoyant force on a submerged or floating object by Archimedes' principle, equal to the weight of the fluid displaced. It depends on the fluid density, gravity, and the displaced volume, not on the object's own material.
notes: V is the volume of fluid displaced, which for a fully submerged body equals its own volume. Use fluid density, not the object's density, in kg/m³.

name: Dynamic Pressure (Bernoulli)
description: Gives the dynamic pressure of a moving fluid, the kinetic-energy contribution per unit volume in Bernoulli's equation. It equals half the fluid density times the square of the flow velocity, so it rises steeply with speed.
notes: This is only the dynamic term, not total pressure; it excludes static and hydrostatic contributions. Assumes incompressible flow, a good approximation for air well below the speed of sound.

name: Bernoulli Total Pressure
description: Sums the three terms of Bernoulli's equation — static pressure, dynamic pressure (half rho v squared), and hydrostatic pressure (rho g h) — to give the total pressure along a streamline. For ideal steady flow this total stays constant along the streamline.
notes: Valid for incompressible, non-viscous, steady flow along a single streamline. All terms must share consistent SI units; h is the height relative to a chosen reference level.

name: Volumetric Flow Rate (Q = A·v)
description: Computes the volumetric flow rate through a cross-section as the product of the cross-sectional area A and the average flow velocity v. It represents the volume of fluid passing the section each second.
notes: Assumes velocity is uniform across the section (or v is the mean velocity). Keep area in m² and velocity in m/s to obtain m³/s.

name: Mass Flow Rate
description: Gives the mass flow rate through a cross-section as the product of fluid density, cross-sectional area, and flow velocity. It is the mass of fluid crossing the section per second, equal to density times the volumetric flow rate.
notes: Assumes uniform density and velocity across the section. Use SI units (kg/m³, m², m/s) to get kilograms per second.

name: Continuity Equation (solve for v2)
description: Uses the continuity equation for incompressible flow to find the outlet velocity from the inlet area, inlet velocity, and outlet area. Because the volume flow rate is conserved, a narrower outlet forces a faster flow.
notes: Valid only for incompressible, steady flow where mass is conserved. Both areas must use the same unit; a smaller outlet area A2 gives a larger v2.

name: Reynolds Number
description: Computes the Reynolds number, a dimensionless ratio of inertial to viscous forces in a flow, from density, velocity, a characteristic length, and dynamic viscosity. It predicts whether flow tends to be laminar or turbulent.
notes: Roughly, pipe flow is laminar below about 2300 and turbulent above about 4000. The characteristic length depends on geometry (e.g. pipe diameter); the result is dimensionless.

name: Pascal's Principle (Pressure = F/A)
description: Gives the pressure produced by a force F applied over an area A, the basic definition of pressure underlying Pascal's principle. The same pressure is transmitted undiminished throughout a confined fluid.
notes: Force in newtons and area in m² give pressure in pascals. Pressure and force are distinct: a small force on a tiny area can yield very high pressure.

name: Hydraulic Press Output Force
description: Calculates the output force of a hydraulic press by multiplying the input force by the ratio of the output to input piston areas. Because pressure is transmitted equally, a larger output piston multiplies the force accordingly.
notes: Both piston areas must use the same unit. Force is multiplied but the output piston moves a proportionally shorter distance, so work (energy) is not increased.

name: Period from Frequency
description: Converts a frequency into the period of one cycle by taking its reciprocal. A frequency of 440 hertz corresponds to a period of about 0.00227 seconds per cycle.
notes: Frequency must be in hertz to yield the period in seconds. This is the exact inverse of the frequency-from-period relation.

name: Photon Energy (E=hf)
description: Gives the energy of a single photon from its frequency using the Planck relation, energy equals Planck's constant times frequency. Higher-frequency light carries proportionally more energy per photon.
notes: Frequency must be in hertz; the resulting energy in joules is extremely small for a single photon. Divide by the electron charge to convert to electron-volts if desired.

name: Photon Energy (E=hc/λ)
description: Computes a photon's energy from its wavelength, using Planck's constant times the speed of light divided by the wavelength. Shorter wavelengths carry more energy, so the energy is inversely proportional to wavelength.
notes: Wavelength must be in meters (e.g. 5e-7 m for green light). Use the speed of light in the medium if not in vacuum; the result is in joules.

name: de Broglie Wavelength
description: Gives the de Broglie wavelength of a particle from its mass and velocity, expressing the wave nature of matter as Planck's constant divided by momentum. Faster or heavier particles have shorter wavelengths.
notes: This non-relativistic form uses momentum m times v; at speeds near light, relativistic momentum is needed. The wavelength is measurable only for very light particles like electrons.

name: Refractive Index (n=c/v)
description: Calculates the refractive index of a medium as the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to its speed in the medium. Light slows in denser optical media, so a higher index means slower propagation.
notes: Both speeds must use the same unit; the result is dimensionless and at least 1 for ordinary media. It describes phase speed reduction, not absorption.

name: Snell's Law (refraction angle)
description: Uses Snell's law to find the angle of refraction when light passes from a medium of index n1 into one of index n2 at incidence angle theta1. Light bends toward the normal when entering a denser (higher-index) medium.
notes: Angles are in radians measured from the surface normal. If n1 sin(theta1) exceeds n2, total internal reflection occurs and no real refraction angle exists (arcsine undefined).

name: Critical Angle
description: Computes the critical angle for total internal reflection at a boundary, where n1 is the denser medium (inside) and n2 the less dense one (outside). Beyond this incidence angle, all light is reflected back into the denser medium.
notes: Requires n1 greater than n2 for a real solution; the result is in radians. At exactly this angle the refracted ray grazes along the interface.

name: Thin Lens (image distance)
description: Solves the thin-lens equation for the image distance given the focal length and object distance. It locates where a lens forms an image, whether real (positive result) or virtual (negative result).
notes: Follows the sign convention where a positive focal length is a converging lens. If the object sits at the focal point, the denominator is zero and the image forms at infinity.

name: Magnification
description: Gives the transverse magnification of an optical system as the negative ratio of image distance to object distance. Its sign shows image orientation and its magnitude shows how much larger or smaller the image is.
notes: A negative result means an inverted image; a magnitude below 1 means the image is reduced. Use the same distance unit and consistent sign convention for both distances.

name: Lensmaker's Equation (focal length)
description: Uses the lensmaker's equation to find the focal length of a thin lens from its refractive index and the radii of curvature of its two surfaces. It links the lens shape and material to its converging or diverging power.
notes: Radii follow a sign convention (positive if the surface center of curvature is on the outgoing side). Assumes a thin lens in air; a positive result is a converging lens.

name: Mirror Equation (image distance)
description: Solves the mirror equation for the image distance of a curved mirror given its focal length and the object distance. It shows where a spherical mirror forms an image of an object.
notes: Uses the sign convention where a concave mirror has positive focal length. A negative image distance indicates a virtual image behind the mirror.

name: Sound Level (decibels)
description: Computes the sound intensity level in decibels as ten times the base-10 logarithm of the intensity relative to a reference intensity. The logarithmic scale compresses the huge range of audible intensities.
notes: The reference i0 is usually 1e-12 W/m², the threshold of hearing. A tenfold increase in intensity raises the level by 10 dB; both intensities must use the same unit.

name: Sound Intensity
description: Gives the sound intensity at distance r from a point source radiating power p uniformly in all directions, by spreading the power over the surface of a sphere of radius r. Intensity falls off as the inverse square of distance.
notes: Assumes a point source with no reflections or absorption in the medium. Doubling the distance cuts the intensity to a quarter; keep power in watts and distance in meters.

name: Doppler Effect (approaching)
description: Gives the frequency heard when a source and observer approach each other, shifting the source frequency upward. The observed frequency rises as the observer speed adds to and the source speed subtracts from the speed of sound in the ratio.
notes: All speeds are relative to the medium (still air) and must be positive for approach in this configuration. Valid only while source speed stays below the speed of sound.

name: Doppler Effect (receding)
description: Gives the frequency heard when a source and observer recede from each other, shifting the source frequency downward. The observer speed subtracts from and the source speed adds to the speed of sound in the ratio, lowering the observed pitch.
notes: All speeds are relative to the medium and taken positive for the receding case. It assumes motion along the line joining source and observer.

name: Diffraction Grating (angle)
description: Uses the diffraction grating equation to find the angle at which the m-th order maximum appears for light of a given wavelength and slit spacing. Longer wavelengths and higher orders diffract to larger angles.
notes: The slit spacing d is the distance between adjacent slits (inverse of lines per meter). No solution exists if m times wavelength exceeds d, since the arcsine argument would exceed 1.

name: Oscillator Wave Energy
description: Computes the total energy of a mechanical oscillator vibrating at frequency f with amplitude a, treating it as simple harmonic motion with angular frequency 2πf. The energy grows with the square of both frequency and amplitude.
notes: Frequency must be in hertz; it is converted internally to angular frequency. The result assumes undamped simple harmonic motion of the given mass.

name: Standing Wave Harmonic (string)
description: Gives the frequency of the n-th harmonic of a standing wave on a string fixed at both ends, from the wave speed and string length. The harmonics are integer multiples of the fundamental frequency (n = 1).
notes: This form assumes a string fixed at both ends (or a pipe open at both ends). Use the wave speed on the string, which generally differs from the speed of sound in air.

name: Speed of Sound in Air
description: Estimates the speed of sound in dry air as a linear function of temperature, starting from about 331 m/s at 0 degrees Celsius and rising roughly 0.6 m/s per degree. At 20 degrees it gives about 343 m/s.
notes: Temperature must be in degrees Celsius. This is a linear approximation valid near everyday temperatures; it ignores humidity and air pressure effects.

name: Angular Frequency
description: Converts an ordinary frequency in hertz into angular frequency in radians per second by multiplying by 2π. It expresses how many radians of phase the oscillation advances each second.
notes: Frequency must be in hertz (cycles per second). Angular frequency ω is 2π times larger than f; do not confuse the two in oscillation formulas.

name: Wave Number
description: Computes the angular wave number, the spatial frequency of a wave, as 2π divided by the wavelength. It gives the number of radians of phase per unit distance along the wave.
notes: This is the angular wave number in rad/m, not the spectroscopic 1/λ convention. Wavelength must be in meters; shorter wavelengths give larger wave numbers.

name: Frequency from Wave Speed
description: Finds the frequency of a wave from its propagation speed and wavelength by dividing the speed by the wavelength. For a fixed speed, shorter wavelengths correspond to higher frequencies.
notes: Use the wave speed in the same medium as the wavelength. This rearranges the basic relation v = f times wavelength; keep speed in m/s and wavelength in meters.

name: Wavelength from Speed & Frequency
description: Finds the wavelength of a wave by dividing its propagation speed by its frequency. Higher-frequency waves have shorter wavelengths when the speed is fixed.
notes: Use the wave speed in the medium of interest and frequency in hertz. This is the standard v = f times wavelength relation solved for wavelength.

name: Malus's Law
description: Gives the intensity of polarized light after passing through a polarizer, as the incident intensity times the square of the cosine of the angle between the light's polarization and the polarizer axis. Aligned axes transmit fully; crossed axes block all light.
notes: The angle theta must be in radians and is measured between the polarization direction and the transmission axis. It applies to already-polarized light, not unpolarized light.

name: Bragg's Law (wavelength)
description: Uses Bragg's law to find the wavelength that satisfies constructive interference for X-rays reflected from crystal planes spaced d apart at Bragg angle theta, for diffraction order n. It underlies X-ray crystallography.
notes: The angle theta is measured from the crystal plane surface, not the normal, and must be in radians. A valid reflection requires the wavelength to fit within 2d divided by n.

name: Beat Frequency
description: Gives the beat frequency produced when two waves of slightly different frequencies interfere, equal to the absolute difference of the two frequencies. It is the rate at which the combined sound swells and fades.
notes: Both frequencies must use the same unit; the absolute value keeps the result positive regardless of order. Beats are only perceptible when the two frequencies are close.

name: Lens Power
description: Computes the optical power of a lens as the reciprocal of its focal length. A shorter focal length yields greater power, expressed in diopters, so a 0.05 m focal length gives 20 D.
notes: Focal length must be entered in meters, not centimeters, for the result to be in diopters. Use a negative focal length for diverging (concave) lenses, which gives negative power.

name: Rayleigh Criterion (angular resolution)
description: Gives the smallest angular separation that a circular aperture can resolve, from diffraction theory. Two point sources closer than 1.22×wavelength/diameter blur together; the result is the limiting angle in radians.
notes: Wavelength and aperture diameter must share the same length unit (meters). The 1.22 factor applies to circular apertures; slits use a factor of 1. Smaller angle means finer resolving power.

name: Speed of Light in Medium
description: Calculates how fast light travels through a transparent medium by dividing the vacuum speed of light by the medium's refractive index. A higher index means slower light, so n=1.33 (water) gives about 2.26×10⁸ m/s.
notes: The refractive index is dimensionless and always at least 1 for ordinary media. This is phase speed; it does not exceed the vacuum value c because n≥1.

name: Photon Momentum
description: Determines the momentum carried by a single photon from its wavelength, using Planck's constant divided by wavelength. Shorter wavelengths carry more momentum; the result is in kg·m/s.
notes: Wavelength must be in meters. This is the de Broglie relation p=h/λ; equivalently p=E/c. Photon momentum is extremely small, so results are on the order of 10⁻²⁷ kg·m/s.

name: Fundamental Frequency of a String
description: Finds the lowest vibration frequency of a stretched string fixed at both ends, from its length, tension, and linear mass density. Higher tension or a shorter, lighter string raises the pitch; the result is in hertz.
notes: Linear density is mass per unit length (kg/m), not total mass. This gives only the fundamental; harmonics are integer multiples. Assumes an ideal, uniform, perfectly flexible string.

name: Moment of Inertia — Solid Sphere
description: Computes the moment of inertia of a uniform solid sphere about an axis through its center as two-fifths of mass times radius squared. It quantifies the sphere's resistance to angular acceleration.
notes: Assumes a uniform-density solid sphere rotating about a central axis. Result is in kg·m² with mass in kg and radius in meters.

name: Moment of Inertia — Hollow Sphere (Thin Shell)
description: Computes the moment of inertia of a thin spherical shell about a central axis as two-thirds of mass times radius squared. A hollow shell resists rotation more than a solid sphere of equal mass and radius.
notes: Assumes a thin shell with all mass at the surface radius; a thick-walled sphere differs. Result is in kg·m² with mass in kg and radius in meters.

name: Moment of Inertia — Solid Cylinder / Disk
description: Computes the moment of inertia of a uniform solid cylinder or disk about its central symmetry axis as one-half of mass times radius squared. It measures resistance to spinning about that axis.
notes: Applies to rotation about the central longitudinal axis; a diameter axis gives a different value. Length does not appear, and the result is in kg·m².

name: Moment of Inertia — Thin Hoop / Ring
description: Computes the moment of inertia of a thin hoop or ring about its central axis as mass times radius squared. With all mass at the rim, it has the largest inertia of the common shapes for a given mass and radius.
notes: Assumes all mass concentrated at radius r and rotation about the axis perpendicular to the hoop's plane through its center. Result is in kg·m².

name: Moment of Inertia — Thick Hollow Cylinder
description: Computes the moment of inertia of a thick-walled hollow cylinder (annular tube) about its central axis as one-half of mass times the sum of the inner and outer radii squared. It accounts for both wall radii.
notes: Both radii must use the same units, with inner radius less than outer. Setting the inner radius to zero recovers the solid-cylinder result; the answer is in kg·m².

name: Moment of Inertia — Solid Cone (About Axis)
description: Gives the mass moment of inertia of a solid cone about its central symmetry axis, equal to 3/10 times the mass times the base radius squared. It measures how strongly the cone resists angular acceleration about that axis.
notes: The axis passes through the apex along the cone's centerline; r is the base radius, not the slant length. Result units are kg·m² and grow with the square of the radius.

name: Moment of Inertia — Rod About Center
description: Computes the moment of inertia of a thin uniform rod rotating about an axis through its center and perpendicular to its length, equal to (1/12)·m·l². It quantifies rotational inertia for that central axis.
notes: Valid for a thin rod where thickness is negligible; l is the full length. Rotation about the end instead uses (1/3)·m·l², four times larger.

name: Moment of Inertia — Rod About End
description: Computes the moment of inertia of a thin uniform rod rotating about an axis through one end and perpendicular to its length, equal to (1/3)·m·l². This is the value used for a rod pivoting at its tip.
notes: l is the full rod length and the axis is at one end, not the center. This inertia is four times the central-axis value (1/12)·m·l².

name: Moment of Inertia — Rectangular Plate (Central Axis)
description: Gives the moment of inertia of a thin rectangular plate about the axis through its center and perpendicular to its face, equal to (1/12)·m·(a²+b²) where a and b are the two side lengths. It measures resistance to spinning about that central axis.
notes: The axis is perpendicular to the plate through its centroid; thickness is assumed negligible. Both side lengths contribute, each squared and summed.

name: Moment of Inertia — Disk About Diameter
description: Computes the moment of inertia of a thin uniform disk about an axis lying along one of its diameters (in the plane of the disk), equal to (1/4)·m·r². It applies when the disk tips about a line through its center.
notes: This is the diameter (in-plane) axis, giving (1/4)·m·r², which is half the perpendicular central-axis value (1/2)·m·r². Assumes a thin disk.

name: Radius of Gyration
description: Returns the radius of gyration, the distance from the rotation axis at which the whole mass could be concentrated to give the same moment of inertia, computed as the square root of I divided by m. It summarizes how mass is distributed relative to the axis.
notes: I must be taken about the same axis of interest and be in kg·m² with m in kg; the result is a length in meters. It is not a physical radius of the body.

name: Parallel Axis Theorem
description: Applies the parallel axis theorem to find the moment of inertia about an axis parallel to one through the center of mass: I = Icm + m·d², where d is the distance between the two axes. It shifts a known central inertia to any parallel axis.
notes: The two axes must be parallel, and Icm must be about the center-of-mass axis. Moving away from the center of mass always increases inertia, since m·d² is added.

name: Torque from Angular Acceleration
description: Computes the net torque required to give a rotating body an angular acceleration, using the rotational form of Newton's second law, τ = I·α. The result is the turning effort in newton-meters.
notes: I and α must be about the same axis; α is in rad/s². This assumes a rigid body with constant moment of inertia about that axis.

name: Angular Acceleration from Torque
description: Solves the rotational Newton's second law for angular acceleration, α = τ / I, giving how quickly the angular velocity changes under an applied torque. The result is in rad/s².
notes: Torque and moment of inertia must refer to the same axis; a larger inertia yields a smaller acceleration for the same torque.

name: Rolling Kinetic Energy (Total)
description: Adds the translational kinetic energy (1/2)·m·v² and the rotational kinetic energy (1/2)·I·ω² to give the total kinetic energy of a rolling body. It captures energy in both linear motion and spin.
notes: For rolling without slipping the speeds are linked by v = ω·r; enter consistent values. I is about the body's own rotation axis and ω is in rad/s.

name: Flywheel Energy from RPM
description: Computes the rotational kinetic energy stored in a flywheel from its moment of inertia and rotational speed in rpm, converting to angular velocity as ω = 2π·n/60 and evaluating (1/2)·I·ω². The result is the stored energy in joules.
notes: Input speed n is in rpm and is converted internally; do not pre-convert to rad/s. Energy scales with the square of the speed, so doubling rpm quadruples the energy.

name: Angular Velocity (Kinematics)
description: Gives the angular velocity after time t under constant angular acceleration, ω = ω0 + α·t, the rotational analogue of v = v0 + a·t. The result is the final angular velocity in rad/s.
notes: Valid only for constant angular acceleration. Keep ω0 and α in the same rotational sense; a negative α represents deceleration.

name: Angular Displacement (Kinematics)
description: Computes the angle swept in time t under constant angular acceleration, θ = ω0·t + (1/2)·α·t², the rotational analogue of the linear displacement equation. The result is the angular displacement in radians.
notes: Assumes constant angular acceleration and consistent rotational sense for ω0 and α. θ is a total swept angle in radians, not reduced to within one revolution.

name: Final Angular Velocity (No Time)
description: Finds the final angular velocity after turning through angle θ under constant angular acceleration without needing the time, using ω = √(ω0² + 2·α·θ). It is the rotational analogue of v² = v0² + 2·a·s.
notes: Requires constant angular acceleration; θ is in radians and α in rad/s². The radicand must be non-negative, so strong deceleration over a large angle can make this invalid.

name: Centripetal Acceleration (Angular)
description: Computes the centripetal (radial) acceleration of a point moving in a circle from its angular velocity and radius, a = ω²·r. This acceleration points toward the center and keeps the point on its circular path.
notes: ω must be in rad/s, not rpm or degrees. This gives only the radial component; any tangential acceleration from changing speed is separate.

name: Centripetal Acceleration from RPM
description: Computes centripetal acceleration for a body rotating at n rpm at radius r by converting to angular velocity ω = 2π·n/60 and evaluating ω²·r. The result is the inward radial acceleration in m/s².
notes: Input speed n is in rpm and converted internally; do not pre-convert. Acceleration rises with the square of rpm, so it grows quickly at high speeds.

name: Rolling Without Slipping
description: Gives the linear speed of the center of a wheel that rolls without slipping, v = ω·r, linking spin rate to travel speed. The contact point is momentarily at rest, so the center moves at exactly ω·r.
notes: Valid only when there is no slipping between wheel and surface. ω must be in rad/s; the same relation gives the contact-point tangential speed.

name: Tangential Acceleration
description: Computes the tangential acceleration of a point on a rotating body from its angular acceleration and radius, a = α·r. This is the along-the-path component that changes the point's speed.
notes: α must be in rad/s². This is distinct from centripetal acceleration ω²·r; the total acceleration combines both components at right angles.

name: Banking Angle of a Curve
description: Finds the ideal banking angle for a curve so that no friction is needed at speed v, θ = arctan(v²/(r·g)), where r is the curve radius and g is gravity. At this angle the horizontal component of the normal force supplies the centripetal force.
notes: The result is in radians and assumes friction-free ideal banking at exactly speed v. Use consistent SI units; at other speeds some friction is required.

name: Gyroscopic Precession Rate
description: Computes the precession angular velocity of a spinning gyroscope under gravity, Ω = m·g·d/(I·ω), where d is the pivot-to-center-of-mass distance and I·ω is the spin angular momentum. It gives how fast the spin axis slowly circles about the vertical.
notes: Valid in the fast-spin approximation where spin ω is much larger than the precession rate. I is the spin-axis moment of inertia and ω is in rad/s.

name: Physical Pendulum Period
description: Computes the small-oscillation period of a physical (rigid-body) pendulum, T = 2π·√(I/(m·g·d)), where I is the moment of inertia about the pivot and d is the pivot-to-center-of-mass distance. It gives the time for one full swing.
notes: Valid only for small-amplitude swings, and I must be taken about the pivot axis, not the center of mass. Larger amplitudes have longer periods than this predicts.

name: Torque from Force and Angle
description: Computes the torque produced by a force applied at a lever arm, τ = r·F·sin(θ), where θ is the angle between the lever arm and the force direction. Only the perpendicular component of the force creates turning effect.
notes: θ must be in radians; torque is maximal at θ = π/2 (90°) and zero when the force is along the arm. Result is in newton-meters.

name: Work Done by Torque
description: Computes the rotational work done by a constant torque acting through an angular displacement, W = τ·θ, the rotational analogue of force times distance. The result is energy in joules.
notes: θ must be in radians, and the torque is assumed constant over the rotation. For a full turn θ = 2π; a varying torque would require integration.

name: Tangential Force from Torque
description: Finds the tangential force at radius r that produces a given torque, F = τ/r, assuming the force acts perpendicular to the radius. It is the effective force at the rim for a known turning moment.
notes: Assumes the force is applied perpendicular to the lever arm at radius r. A larger radius gives a smaller required force for the same torque.

name: Lever — Effort Force
description: Computes the effort force needed to balance a load on a lever, F = load·(load arm)/(effort arm), from the principle of moments. A longer effort arm relative to the load arm reduces the required effort.
notes: This is the ideal (frictionless, weightless-lever) balance value; real levers need slightly more. Both arm lengths are measured from the fulcrum.

name: Inclined Plane — Effort Force
description: Computes the effort force to move a load up a frictionless inclined plane, F = load·h/l, where h is the height gained and l is the slope length. The incline trades a smaller force over a longer distance.
notes: Ideal frictionless result and it assumes the effort acts parallel to the slope. The load here is a weight in newtons; friction would increase the real effort.

name: Inclined Plane — Mechanical Advantage
description: Gives the ideal mechanical advantage of an inclined plane as the ratio of slope length to height, MA = l/h. It shows how many times the effort force is multiplied compared with lifting straight up.
notes: This is the ideal, frictionless mechanical advantage; friction lowers the actual value. The result is a dimensionless ratio greater than one for a genuine ramp.

name: Wheel and Axle — Effort Force
description: Computes the effort force applied at the wheel to raise a load on the axle, F = load·(axle radius)/(wheel radius), from the balance of torques. A larger wheel radius relative to the axle reduces the effort needed.
notes: Ideal frictionless value; the ratio of radii equals the mechanical advantage. Effort is applied at the wheel rim and the load hangs from the axle.

name: Screw / Jack — Effort Force
description: Computes the ideal effort force at the handle of a screw jack, F = load·p/(2π·r), where p is the thread pitch and r is the handle radius. One turn moves the load by one pitch while the effort travels 2π·r.
notes: Ideal frictionless value; real screw jacks lose much of this advantage to friction (which also provides self-locking). Pitch p and radius r must be in the same length units.

name: Wedge — Mechanical Advantage
description: Gives the ideal mechanical advantage of a wedge as the ratio of its slope length to its thickness, MA = l/t. A long, thin wedge multiplies the driving force more strongly.
notes: Ideal, frictionless ratio; friction (needed to keep a wedge in place) reduces the real advantage. The result is a dimensionless ratio.

name: Pulley System — Effort Force
description: Computes the effort force in an ideal block-and-tackle, F = load/n, where n is the number of rope segments supporting the load. Sharing the load across more segments lowers the pull required.
notes: Ideal frictionless, weightless-rope value; count only the rope segments that actually support the moving load. Real systems need more effort due to friction.

name: Gear Train Ratio
description: Computes the gear ratio of a simple gear train as the number of driven-gear teeth divided by driver-gear teeth, i = Tout/Tin. A ratio above one means torque is multiplied and output speed reduced.
notes: The result is dimensionless; output speed is divided and torque multiplied by this same ratio (ideal, lossless). Tooth counts are whole numbers.

name: Gear Output Speed
description: Computes the output angular speed of a gear pair from the input speed and tooth counts, ωout = ωin·Tin/Tout. A larger driven gear (more teeth) turns more slowly than the driver.
notes: Ideal, lossless relation; the output keeps the input's angular units (here rad/s). Torque changes inversely, rising as speed falls.

name: Belt / Pulley Surface Speed
description: Computes the surface (belt) speed at the rim of a pulley from its diameter and rotational speed in rpm, v = π·d·n/60. This is the linear speed of the belt running over the pulley.
notes: Speed n is in rpm and converted internally; d is the diameter, not the radius. The /60 converts revolutions per minute to per second.

name: Belt Drive — Driven Speed
description: Computes the rotational speed of the driven pulley in a belt drive, n2 = n1·d1/d2, from the driver speed and the two pulley diameters. A larger driven pulley turns more slowly than the driver.
notes: Assumes no belt slip; output speed keeps the input rpm units. Diameters may be replaced by radii since only their ratio matters.

name: Tipping / Toppling Angle
description: Computes the tilt angle at which an object begins to topple, θ = arctan(b/h), where b is the half base width and h is the center-of-mass height. Beyond this angle the vertical through the center of mass falls outside the base.
notes: The result is in radians and assumes tipping about a base edge with no sliding. A wider base or lower center of mass raises the toppling angle.

name: Center of Mass — Two Bodies
description: Computes the position of the center of mass of two point masses along a line, x = (m1·x1 + m2·x2)/(m1 + m2). It is the mass-weighted average of the two positions.
notes: Positions are measured on a common axis and may be negative; the result lies between x1 and x2, nearer the heavier mass. Extends to more bodies by adding terms.

name: Photoelectric Effect (Max Kinetic Energy)
description: Computes the maximum kinetic energy of an ejected photoelectron from Einstein's photoelectric equation, KEmax = h·f − φ, where h·f is the photon energy and φ is the material's work function. The result is the leftover energy after freeing the electron.
notes: If h·f is below the work function φ the result is negative, meaning no electrons are emitted. All energies here are in joules and f is in hertz.

name: Stopping Potential
description: Computes the stopping potential in the photoelectric effect, V = (h·f − φ)/qe, the voltage that just halts the most energetic photoelectrons. It equals the maximum electron kinetic energy divided by the elementary charge.
notes: Meaningful only when h·f exceeds the work function φ; otherwise no emission occurs. Energies are in joules and qe in coulombs, giving volts.

name: Threshold Frequency
description: Computes the threshold frequency for the photoelectric effect, f0 = φ/h, the minimum light frequency that can eject electrons from a material with work function φ. Below this frequency no photoemission occurs.
notes: φ is in joules and h in J·s, giving f0 in hertz. Frequencies at or above f0 are required regardless of light intensity.

name: Work Function from Threshold
description: Computes a material's work function from its threshold frequency, φ = h·f0, the minimum energy needed to free an electron from the surface. It is the photon energy exactly at the emission threshold.
notes: f0 is in hertz and h in J·s, so φ comes out in joules; divide by 1.602e−19 to express it in electron-volts.

name: Max Photoelectron Speed
description: Computes the maximum speed of an ejected photoelectron by equating its kinetic energy to h·f − φ, giving v = √(2·(h·f − φ)/m). It converts the leftover photon energy into electron speed.
notes: Requires h·f greater than φ, or the radicand is negative and no electrons escape. This is a non-relativistic estimate; m is the electron mass in kg.

name: Planck Energy Quantum
description: Computes the energy of a single quantum (photon) of radiation from its frequency using the Planck relation, E = h·f. It gives the smallest packet of energy carried by light of that frequency.
notes: f is in hertz and h in J·s, giving energy in joules. Energy scales linearly with frequency, so higher-frequency light carries more energy per photon.

name: Photon Energy from Wavelength
description: Computes photon energy from its wavelength using E = h·c/λ, combining the Planck relation with c = f·λ. Shorter wavelengths correspond to higher-energy photons.
notes: λ is in meters and the result is in joules; use the vacuum speed of light for c. Energy is inversely proportional to wavelength.

name: Bohr Energy Level
description: Computes the energy of an electron in level n of a hydrogen-like atom in the Bohr model, E = −13.6·z²/n² electron-volts, where z is the atomic number. The negative sign indicates the electron is bound to the nucleus.
notes: Applies to single-electron (hydrogen-like) atoms only; n is a positive integer. The result is in eV, and energy approaches zero as n grows large.

name: Bohr Orbit Radius
description: Computes the radius of the electron's orbit in level n of a hydrogen-like atom in the Bohr model, r = a0·n²/z, where a0 is the Bohr radius and z the atomic number. The orbit grows with the square of the level number.
notes: Valid for single-electron atoms; n is a positive integer and a0 ≈ 5.29e−11 m. Higher nuclear charge z pulls the orbit inward.

name: Bohr Orbital Velocity
description: Computes the electron's orbital speed in level n of a hydrogen-like atom in the Bohr model, v = 2.188e6·z/n m/s, where the constant is the ground-state speed of hydrogen. The electron moves slower in higher levels.
notes: Applies to single-electron atoms; n is a positive integer. The constant 2,188,000 m/s is roughly the fine-structure constant times the speed of light.

name: Hydrogen Transition Energy
description: Computes the energy released or absorbed when an electron moves between two levels in a hydrogen-like atom, ΔE = 13.6·z²·(1/n1² − 1/n2²) electron-volts. A positive value corresponds to emission from the upper to the lower level.
notes: n1 is the lower level and n2 the upper; the result is in eV. This assumes single-electron (hydrogen-like) atoms in the Bohr model.

name: Rydberg Wavelength
description: Computes the wavelength of light emitted or absorbed in a hydrogen transition using the Rydberg formula, λ = 1/(R·(1/n1² − 1/n2²)), where R is the Rydberg constant. It links the two energy levels to a spectral line.
notes: n1 is the lower level and n2 the upper (n2 > n1) so the denominator is positive. R is in 1/m, giving λ in meters.

name: Mass-Energy Equivalence (E=mc^2)
description: Computes the rest energy equivalent of a mass using Einstein's relation E = m·c², the total energy contained in a mass at rest. Even a tiny mass corresponds to an enormous energy because c is squared.
notes: m is in kg and c is the speed of light in m/s, giving energy in joules. This is rest energy; kinetic energy from motion is additional.

name: Rest Energy in eV
description: Computes the rest energy of a particle, E = m·c², and expresses it in electron-volts by dividing the joule value by the elementary charge. For an electron this gives about 511000 eV (0.511 MeV).
notes: Mass must be in kilograms and c in metres per second so the energy is in joules before the division. Dividing by qe (in coulombs) converts joules to eV, not to keV or MeV.

name: Mass Defect Binding Energy
description: Applies E = Δm·c² to convert a nuclear mass defect into its equivalent binding energy in joules. The mass defect is the difference between the summed masses of the free nucleons and the actual nuclear mass.
notes: The mass defect must be entered in kilograms; if given in atomic mass units it has to be converted first. The result is the total binding energy of the whole nucleus, not per nucleon.

name: Binding Energy from Mass Defect (MeV)
description: Converts a mass defect expressed in atomic mass units directly into binding energy in MeV, using the conversion factor that one unified mass unit equals about 931.5 MeV/c². It is a shortcut for E = Δm·c².
notes: The mass defect must be in atomic mass units (u), not kilograms. The factor 931.5 already includes c², so no further multiplication by the speed of light is needed.

name: Binding Energy per Nucleon
description: Divides the total nuclear binding energy by the mass number to give the average binding energy holding each nucleon in the nucleus. This value peaks near iron and indicates nuclear stability.
notes: The mass number A is the total count of protons and neutrons and is dimensionless. Keep the total binding energy in MeV so the result comes out in MeV per nucleon.

name: Nuclear Radius
description: Estimates the radius of an atomic nucleus using R = r0·A^(1/3), where the cube root of the mass number reflects that nuclear volume is roughly proportional to the number of nucleons. The result is a length in metres.
notes: The mass number A is dimensionless; the radius constant r0 (about 1.2 femtometres) sets the scale. This is an empirical approximation assuming a nearly constant nuclear density.

name: Radioactive Decay Law
description: Gives the number of undecayed nuclei remaining after time t through exponential decay, N = N0·exp(−λt), where λ is the decay constant. The population falls to 1/e of its start after a time 1/λ.
notes: The decay constant λ and the time t must use consistent time units so that λt is dimensionless. This assumes a single decay mode with a constant probability per nucleus.

name: Radioactive Activity
description: Calculates the activity of a radioactive sample, A = λ·N, the number of decays per second produced by N nuclei each with decay constant λ. The result is in becquerels (decays per second).
notes: The decay constant must be in inverse seconds so the activity comes out in becquerels. Activity is proportional to the number of nuclei present, so it decreases as the sample decays.

name: Half-life to Decay Constant
description: Converts a half-life into the corresponding decay constant using λ = ln(2)/t½. The decay constant is the probability per unit time that a given nucleus decays.
notes: The result carries the inverse of whatever time unit the half-life uses, so a half-life in seconds gives a decay constant in inverse seconds. ln(2) is about 0.693.

name: Decay Constant to Half-life
description: Converts a decay constant into the half-life through t½ = ln(2)/λ, the time over which half of a large sample of nuclei decays. It is the inverse of the half-life-to-decay-constant relation.
notes: The half-life comes out in the time unit matching the decay constant, so a λ in inverse seconds yields a half-life in seconds. Half-life is independent of the amount of material present.

name: Compton Shift
description: Gives the increase in photon wavelength after Compton scattering off a stationary electron, Δλ = h/(m·c)·(1 − cos θ), where θ is the scattering angle. The shift is largest for back-scattering (θ = π).
notes: The scattering angle must be in radians. The shift depends only on the angle, not on the incident wavelength, and is zero for forward scattering (θ = 0).

name: Compton Wavelength
description: Computes the Compton wavelength of a particle, λ = h/(m·c), a fundamental length scale set by its mass. For the electron it is about 2.43 picometres.
notes: Mass must be in kilograms and c in metres per second to give a length in metres. This is the maximum possible Compton shift divided by two, and it shrinks for heavier particles.

name: de Broglie Momentum
description: Finds the momentum associated with a matter wave of a given wavelength, p = h/λ, from de Broglie's relation. Shorter wavelengths correspond to larger momenta.
notes: The wavelength must be in metres so the momentum comes out in kilogram-metres per second. This links a wave property to a particle property and applies to any matter wave or photon.

name: de Broglie Wavelength (Accelerated Electron)
description: Gives the de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated from rest through a voltage U, λ = h/√(2·m·qe·U). The denominator is the non-relativistic momentum gained from the electric field.
notes: The accelerating voltage is in volts and the result is in metres. This is a non-relativistic approximation and becomes inaccurate at very high voltages where the electron speed approaches c.

name: Heisenberg Uncertainty (Momentum)
description: Estimates the minimum uncertainty in momentum consistent with a given position uncertainty, using the Heisenberg limit Δp = ħ/(2·Δx). Smaller position uncertainty forces larger momentum uncertainty.
notes: This gives the lower bound of the product Δx·Δp = ħ/2, not an exact value, so real momentum spreads can be larger. Position uncertainty in metres yields momentum in kilogram-metres per second.

name: Relativistic Total Energy
description: Computes the total relativistic energy of a moving particle, E = m·c²/√(1 − v²/c²), which includes both its rest energy and kinetic energy. The energy diverges as the speed approaches c.
notes: The velocity must be less than the speed of light or the square root becomes undefined. Here m is the rest mass, and subtracting m·c² would give the relativistic kinetic energy.

name: Relativistic Mass
description: Gives the velocity-dependent relativistic mass, m = m0/√(1 − v²/c²), which grows without bound as the speed approaches the speed of light. At low speeds it reduces to the rest mass m0.
notes: The speed must be below c so the denominator stays real and positive. Relativistic mass is an older convention; many modern treatments keep mass invariant and put the gamma factor with energy and momentum.

name: Energy-Momentum Relation
description: Applies the relativistic energy-momentum relation E = √((p·c)² + (m·c²)²) to find a particle's total energy from its momentum and rest mass. For a massless particle it reduces to E = p·c.
notes: Momentum in kilogram-metres per second and mass in kilograms give energy in joules. This holds for any speed and does not require knowing the velocity directly.

name: Time Dilation
description: Gives the dilated time interval measured in a frame where a clock moves, t = t0/√(1 − v²/c²), from the proper time t0 measured in the clock's own frame. Moving clocks are observed to run slow.
notes: The velocity must be less than c. The proper time t0 is the interval between two events measured at the same place in the clock's rest frame; the result is always longer than t0.

name: Proper Time
description: Recovers the proper time t0 = t·√(1 − v²/c²) from an observed time interval t in a frame where the clock moves at speed v. It is the time elapsed on the moving clock itself.
notes: The speed must be below c. Proper time is always shorter than the observed interval, and this is the inverse of the time-dilation relation.

name: Relativistic Velocity Addition
description: Combines two collinear velocities relativistically, (u1 + u2)/(1 + u1·u2/c²), so the result never exceeds the speed of light. At low speeds it reduces to the ordinary sum u1 + u2.
notes: Both velocities must be along the same line and below c; opposite directions need one entered as negative. Adding any speed to c still gives exactly c.

name: Relativistic Doppler Effect
description: Gives the observed frequency for relative motion along the line of sight, f = f0·√((1 + β)/(1 − β)), where β = v/c. As written, a positive β corresponds to approach and a blueshift.
notes: β is the speed as a fraction of c and must be between −1 and 1; use a negative value for recession (redshift). This longitudinal form ignores the purely transverse Doppler effect.

name: Gravitational Time Dilation
description: Gives the time interval measured by a clock at radius r near a mass, t = t0·√(1 − 2·G·M/(r·c²)), relative to a far-away clock reading t0. Clocks deeper in a gravitational well run slower.
notes: This Schwarzschild result assumes a non-rotating spherical mass and a clock at rest outside it. The term 2GM/(rc²) must be less than one, i.e. r must exceed the Schwarzschild radius.

name: Planck Length
description: Evaluates the Planck length √(ħ·G/c³), the fundamental length scale formed from the quantum constant ħ, the gravitational constant G, and the speed of light. It is about 1.6×10⁻³⁵ metres.
notes: Using the standard constant values reproduces the fixed Planck length; the variables are exposed only to show its construction. Below this scale, quantum-gravity effects are expected to dominate.

name: Magnifier Angular Magnification
description: Gives the angular magnification of a simple magnifier with the image at the near point, M = 25/f, where f is the focal length in centimetres and 25 cm is the standard near-point distance.
notes: The focal length must be in centimetres because 25 is the near-point distance in centimetres. This assumes a relaxed eye viewing at the conventional 25 cm near point.

name: Telescope Magnification
description: Computes the angular magnification of a refracting telescope in normal adjustment, M = fo/fe, the ratio of the objective focal length to the eyepiece focal length. Longer objectives or shorter eyepieces give more magnification.
notes: Both focal lengths must be in the same unit so the ratio is dimensionless. This assumes the telescope is focused for a relaxed eye with the final image at infinity.

name: Compound Microscope Magnification
description: Gives the total magnification of a compound microscope, (L/fo)·(25/fe), the product of the objective magnification set by the tube length L and the eyepiece magnification. It multiplies two stages of enlargement.
notes: All lengths must be in centimetres to match the 25 cm near-point term. L is the optical tube length between the focal points, and the eye is assumed relaxed.

name: Numerical Aperture
description: Computes the numerical aperture NA = n·sin θ of an optical system, where n is the refractive index of the medium and θ is the half-angle of the maximum cone of light accepted. Larger NA means finer resolving power.
notes: The half-angle must be in radians. NA is dimensionless and cannot exceed the medium's refractive index, which is why immersion media with n above 1 raise the achievable aperture.

name: Rayleigh Angular Resolution
description: Gives the smallest angular separation resolvable by a circular aperture, θ = 1.22·λ/d, from the Rayleigh criterion. Longer wavelengths or smaller apertures give a coarser (larger) resolution angle.
notes: Wavelength and aperture diameter must share the same length unit so the result is in radians. The factor 1.22 is specific to a circular aperture and reflects its diffraction pattern.

name: Brewster's Angle
description: Computes Brewster's angle, θ = arctan(n2/n1), the angle of incidence at which light reflected from a boundary is completely polarised. n1 is the incident medium index and n2 the refracting medium index.
notes: The refractive indices are dimensionless and their order matters; swapping them gives the complementary situation. The result is in radians and is measured from the surface normal.

name: Thin-Film Constructive Thickness (min)
