description: Gives the minimum film thickness λ/(2·n) for constructive interference in reflection when there is a half-wave phase shift at only one surface. λ is the vacuum wavelength and n the film's refractive index.
notes: This specific form assumes a single half-wave phase shift (a low-high-low index stack) and near-normal incidence. The vacuum wavelength is divided by n because the wave is shorter inside the film.

name: Double-Slit Fringe Spacing
description: Computes the spacing between adjacent bright fringes in a double-slit interference pattern, Δy = λ·L/d, where L is the slit-to-screen distance and d the slit separation. Wider slit separation gives closer fringes.
notes: This small-angle approximation assumes the screen is far from the slits (L much greater than d). All lengths must use the same unit so the fringe spacing comes out in metres.

name: Diffraction Grating Angle (1st order)
description: Gives the diffraction angle θ = arcsin(m·λ/d) at which a grating with line spacing d sends order m of wavelength λ. Larger orders and longer wavelengths diffract to greater angles.
notes: The argument m·λ/d must not exceed one, otherwise that order does not exist. Wavelength and grating spacing must share a unit, and the result is in radians from the normal.

name: Lens Power (Diopters)
description: Computes the optical power of a lens, P = 1/f, the reciprocal of its focal length. A short focal length means strong bending of light and a high power in dioptres.
notes: The focal length must be in metres for the power to be in dioptres. A converging lens has positive power and a diverging lens has negative power.

name: Combined Lens Power (in contact)
description: Gives the combined optical power of two thin lenses in contact, P = p1 + p2, since their powers add directly. This determines the effective focal length of the pair.
notes: This simple sum holds only for thin lenses placed in contact with negligible separation; a finite gap requires a correction term. Both powers are in dioptres, with diverging lenses entered as negative.

name: f-Number
description: Computes the f-number N = f/d of a lens, the ratio of focal length to aperture diameter. A larger f-number means a smaller aperture, less light gathered, and greater depth of field.
notes: Focal length and aperture diameter must share the same unit so the result is dimensionless. The light-gathering area scales as 1/N², so doubling N cuts the light to a quarter.

name: Hyperfocal Distance
description: Gives the hyperfocal distance H = f²/(N·c) + f, the focus distance at which depth of field extends from half of H to infinity. N is the f-number and c the circle of confusion.
notes: Focal length and circle of confusion must use the same length unit, and the result carries that unit. A smaller acceptable circle of confusion or larger aperture pushes the hyperfocal distance farther.

name: Critical Angle (total internal reflection)
description: Computes the critical angle θ = arcsin(n2/n1) beyond which light in a denser medium (index n1) undergoes total internal reflection at a boundary with a rarer medium (index n2). Above this angle no light is transmitted.
notes: It requires n1 greater than n2 so the ratio is below one; otherwise no critical angle exists. The result is in radians and measured from the surface normal.

name: Single-Slit First Minimum Angle
description: Gives the angle to the first diffraction minimum of a single slit, θ = arcsin(λ/a), where λ is the wavelength and a the slit width. Narrower slits spread the diffraction pattern to larger angles.
notes: Wavelength and slit width must share a unit, and λ/a must not exceed one. The result is in radians and marks the first dark fringe, not a bright one.

name: Bragg Diffraction Angle
description: Computes the Bragg angle θ = arcsin(m·λ/(2·d)) at which X-rays of wavelength λ diffract constructively from crystal planes spaced by d. The condition is m·λ = 2·d·sin θ.
notes: The angle is measured between the incident beam and the crystal plane, not the normal. The argument m·λ/(2·d) must not exceed one, and wavelength and spacing must share a unit.

name: Solenoid Magnetic Field
description: Gives the magnetic flux density inside a long solenoid, B = μ0·n·i, where n is the number of turns per metre and i the current. The field is nearly uniform along the axis and independent of the radius.
notes: n must be turns per metre, not the total number of turns. This ideal-solenoid result assumes a long coil and ignores end effects near the openings.

name: Toroid Magnetic Field
description: Computes the magnetic field inside a toroid, B = μ0·N·i/(2·π·r), where N is the total number of turns and r the distance from the toroid axis. The field circulates within the ring and varies with r.
notes: N is the total turn count, and r is the mean radius at which the field is evaluated, not the coil cross-section radius. The field is essentially zero outside an ideal toroid.

name: Force Between Parallel Wires (per length)
description: Gives the force per unit length between two parallel current-carrying wires, μ0·i1·i2/(2·π·d), where d is their separation. Currents in the same direction attract and opposite currents repel.
notes: The result is a force per metre, not a total force; multiply by the wire length for the whole force. The sign of the effect depends on the relative current directions, which the magnitude formula does not capture.

name: Magnetic Field of Straight Wire
description: Computes the magnetic flux density at distance r from a long straight wire, B = μ0·i/(2·π·r). The field forms circles around the wire and falls off inversely with distance.
notes: This assumes an infinitely long, thin straight wire and gives the field only outside it. Distance in metres and current in amperes give the result in teslas.

name: Magnetic Field at Loop Centre
description: Gives the magnetic flux density at the centre of a single circular current loop, B = μ0·i/(2·r), where r is the loop radius. Smaller loops or larger currents give a stronger central field.
notes: This applies at the exact centre of a single turn; for N turns multiply by N. The field elsewhere along the axis is weaker and requires the full on-axis formula.

name: Magnetic Dipole Moment
description: Computes the magnetic dipole moment of a current loop, m = N·i·A, the product of the number of turns, the current, and the enclosed area. It sets the torque the loop feels in an external magnetic field.
notes: The area must be in square metres and is the area enclosed by one turn, not the wire cross-section. The moment is a vector normal to the loop; this gives only its magnitude.

name: Hall Voltage
description: Gives the Hall voltage across a conductor, i·b/(nq·q·t), that develops when current i flows through a sample of thickness t in a perpendicular magnetic field b. It reveals the sign and density of charge carriers.
notes: nq is the carrier number density per cubic metre and t is the sample dimension along the field. The magnetic field must be perpendicular to the current for this simple form to apply.

name: Lorentz Force on Moving Charge
description: Computes the magnetic force on a moving charge, F = q·v·b·sin θ, where θ is the angle between the velocity and the magnetic field. The force is maximal when motion is perpendicular to the field and zero when parallel.
notes: The angle must be in radians. This is only the magnetic part of the Lorentz force; the force is always perpendicular to both velocity and field, so it does no work on the charge.

name: Larmor Radiated Power
description: Gives the power radiated by an accelerating point charge, P = q²·a²/(6·π·ε0·c³), from the Larmor formula. The radiated power grows with the square of the acceleration.
notes: This is the non-relativistic Larmor result; at speeds near c it needs the relativistic (Liénard) generalisation. Charge in coulombs and acceleration in metres per second squared give power in watts.

name: Poynting Vector Magnitude
description: Computes the magnitude of the Poynting vector, S = E·B/μ0, the instantaneous power per unit area carried by an electromagnetic wave with fields E and B. It points in the direction of energy flow.
notes: This uses instantaneous field values; for a sinusoidal wave the time-averaged intensity is half the peak value. E and B are the perpendicular field magnitudes and are related by E = c·B in vacuum.

name: Radiation Pressure (absorption)
description: Gives the radiation pressure exerted by light on a fully absorbing surface, p = I/c, where I is the incident intensity. For a perfectly reflecting surface the pressure would be twice as large.
notes: This form assumes complete absorption at normal incidence; reflection doubles it and oblique incidence reduces it. Intensity in watts per square metre gives pressure in pascals.

name: Fresnel Reflectance (normal incidence)
description: Computes the fraction of light intensity reflected at a flat interface between two media at normal incidence, from their refractive indices n1 and n2. The dimensionless result ranges from 0 to 1, so 0.04 means 4 percent of the power is reflected.
notes: Valid only for normal (perpendicular) incidence and non-absorbing media; at oblique angles use the full Fresnel equations. The result is symmetric in n1 and n2, and assumes real refractive indices.

name: Drag Force
description: Gives the aerodynamic or hydrodynamic drag force on a body moving through a fluid, as one half times fluid density times velocity squared times drag coefficient times reference area. The force in newtons acts opposite to the direction of motion.
notes: Force grows with the square of velocity, so doubling speed quadruples drag. The drag coefficient and reference area must be defined consistently for the same body and Reynolds-number regime.

name: Lift Force
description: Calculates the lift force generated by a wing or lifting surface moving through a fluid, as one half times fluid density times velocity squared times lift coefficient times wing area. The result in newtons acts perpendicular to the flow direction.
notes: The lift coefficient depends on angle of attack and airfoil shape and is not constant. Lift scales with velocity squared, and this form assumes incompressible, attached flow below stall.

name: Terminal Velocity
description: Finds the steady falling speed at which drag force balances gravity for an object in a fluid, as the square root of two times mass times gravity divided by the product of fluid density, cross-sectional area and drag coefficient. The result is in meters per second.
notes: Applies to the constant-velocity limit where net force is zero, using a fixed drag coefficient. Heavier or more compact objects reach higher terminal speeds; denser fluids reduce it.

name: Stokes Drag
description: Computes the viscous drag force on a small sphere moving slowly through a fluid, as six times pi times dynamic viscosity times sphere radius times velocity. The result in newtons is proportional to speed, unlike high-speed quadratic drag.
notes: Valid only in the creeping-flow regime at very low Reynolds number (roughly below 1) for a rigid sphere. At higher speeds inertial effects dominate and this underestimates the drag.

name: Poiseuille Flow Rate
description: Gives the volumetric flow rate of a viscous fluid through a circular pipe under laminar conditions, as pi times radius to the fourth power times pressure difference divided by eight times viscosity times length. The result is in cubic meters per second.
notes: Flow depends on the fourth power of radius, so small diameter changes have large effects. Valid only for steady, laminar, fully developed flow of a Newtonian fluid; turbulence breaks this relation.

name: Froude Number
description: Computes the dimensionless Froude number, the ratio of flow inertia to gravity, as velocity divided by the square root of gravity times a characteristic length. Values below 1 indicate subcritical flow and above 1 supercritical flow.
notes: The characteristic length is typically flow depth for open channels. Use the correct length scale for your problem, since the threshold at Fr equals 1 marks the critical-flow transition.

name: Mach Number
description: Gives the Mach number, the dimensionless ratio of an object's speed to the local speed of sound, as velocity divided by sound speed. Values below 1 are subsonic, near 1 transonic, and above 1 supersonic.
notes: The speed of sound depends on the medium and its temperature, so use the local value, not a fixed constant. Compressibility effects become important as the ratio approaches 1.

name: Dynamic Pressure
description: Calculates the dynamic pressure of a moving fluid, the kinetic-energy contribution to Bernoulli's equation, as one half times fluid density times velocity squared. The result in pascals represents the pressure rise when the flow is brought to rest.
notes: This is not the static or total pressure but the velocity-related part. It assumes incompressible flow, so it loses accuracy at high Mach numbers where density changes matter.

name: Torricelli Velocity
description: Gives the ideal efflux velocity of a fluid jet leaving an opening under a head of height h, as the square root of two times gravity times head. The result in meters per second equals the speed a body would reach falling freely through the same height.
notes: Assumes an ideal, frictionless fluid and neglects viscosity and contraction of the jet. Real discharge is lower, which is accounted for with a discharge coefficient.

name: Darcy-Weisbach Pressure Drop
description: Computes the frictional pressure drop for fluid flowing through a pipe, as the friction factor times length over diameter times the dynamic pressure (one half density times velocity squared). The result in pascals is the energy loss due to wall friction.
notes: The friction factor depends on Reynolds number and pipe roughness and must be chosen accordingly. Applies to fully developed flow in a uniform pipe; use a separate approach for fittings and bends.

name: Hydraulic Radius
description: Gives the hydraulic radius of a channel or conduit, defined as the flow cross-sectional area divided by the wetted perimeter. The result in meters characterizes the flow geometry and feeds into open-channel and friction formulas.
notes: The wetted perimeter includes only the boundary in contact with the fluid, not the free surface. It differs from a geometric radius; for a full circular pipe it equals one quarter of the diameter.

name: Manning Velocity
description: Estimates the average velocity of open-channel flow using Manning's formula, as one over the roughness coefficient times hydraulic radius to the two-thirds power times the square root of channel slope. The result is in meters per second.
notes: This is the SI form with an implicit coefficient of 1; imperial units require a factor of 1.49. The roughness coefficient n is empirical and slope should be the energy or bed slope for uniform flow.

name: Pump Hydraulic Power
description: Computes the hydraulic (useful) power delivered by a pump to a fluid, as fluid density times gravity times volumetric flow rate times pump head. The result in watts is the rate of energy imparted to the flow.
notes: This is the ideal hydraulic power, not the shaft or electrical input; dividing by pump efficiency gives the actual power required. Head must be the total dynamic head across the pump.

name: Pressure Head
description: Converts a fluid pressure into an equivalent column height, as pressure divided by the product of fluid density and gravity. The result in meters is the height of fluid whose weight produces that pressure.
notes: Uses gauge pressure relative to the local reference; the value depends on the fluid density chosen. It expresses static pressure only, excluding velocity and elevation contributions.

name: Capillary Rise (Jurin's Law)
description: Predicts the height a liquid rises (or falls) in a narrow tube due to surface tension, as two times surface tension times the cosine of the contact angle divided by liquid density, gravity and tube radius. The result is in meters.
notes: The contact angle must be in radians; angles above 90 degrees give a negative result (depression). Assumes a thin cylindrical tube where capillary effects dominate over the liquid weight.

name: Weber Number
description: Gives the dimensionless Weber number, the ratio of fluid inertia to surface tension, as density times velocity squared times a characteristic length divided by surface tension. High values mean inertia dominates, favoring droplet or interface breakup.
notes: Useful in atomization, sprays and multiphase flows to judge droplet stability. The characteristic length must match the relevant scale, such as droplet diameter, for the number to be meaningful.

name: Young-Laplace Capillary Pressure
description: Computes the pressure difference across the curved surface of a spherical droplet or bubble, as two times surface tension divided by radius. The result in pascals is the excess internal pressure caused by surface tension.
notes: This 2*gamma/r form is for a single spherical interface (a droplet); a soap bubble with two surfaces uses 4*gamma/r. Smaller radii produce much larger pressure differences.

name: Newtonian Shear Stress
description: Gives the shear stress in a Newtonian fluid under simple shear, as dynamic viscosity times the velocity difference divided by the gap distance (the velocity gradient). The result in pascals is the tangential stress resisting the shearing.
notes: Valid only for Newtonian fluids where stress is proportional to shear rate, and for a linear velocity profile across the gap. Non-Newtonian fluids need a different constitutive relation.

name: Specific Weight
description: Computes the specific weight (weight per unit volume) of a fluid, as fluid density times gravitational acceleration. The result in newtons per cubic meter is the gravitational force acting on each unit volume of the fluid.
notes: Specific weight depends on local gravity, unlike density, and differs from specific gravity, which is a dimensionless ratio to water. For water it is about 9810 N/m^3.

name: Orifice Discharge
description: Calculates the volumetric flow rate through an orifice under a head h, as the discharge coefficient times orifice area times the square root of two times gravity times head. The result is in cubic meters per second.
notes: The discharge coefficient (typically around 0.6) corrects the ideal Torricelli velocity for jet contraction and friction. Assumes a constant head and free discharge to atmosphere.

name: Venturi Flow Rate
description: Computes the flow rate through a venturi meter from the pressure drop between inlet and throat, as the discharge coefficient times throat area times the square root of two times pressure difference over density and the area-ratio factor. The result is in cubic meters per second.
notes: The factor 1-(a2/a1)^2 accounts for the upstream velocity, so the inlet and throat areas must be entered correctly. Assumes incompressible, steady flow; the discharge coefficient corrects for real losses.

name: Continuity Velocity
description: Gives the average flow velocity from the continuity equation, as volumetric flow rate divided by cross-sectional area. The result in meters per second is the mean speed of fluid passing through the section.
notes: Assumes incompressible flow and uniform velocity across the section, giving the mean rather than the local peak velocity. For a given flow rate, a smaller area means a proportionally higher velocity.

name: Knudsen Number
description: Computes the dimensionless Knudsen number, the ratio of the molecular mean free path to a characteristic length. It gauges how rarefied a gas is: small values indicate continuum flow, large values free-molecular flow.
notes: Continuum assumptions hold below about 0.01; between 0.1 and 10 flow is transitional and needs slip or kinetic models. The characteristic length should reflect the smallest relevant flow dimension.

name: Euler Number
description: Gives the dimensionless Euler number, the ratio of pressure forces to inertial forces, as pressure difference divided by density times velocity squared. It characterizes pressure losses relative to the dynamic pressure of the flow.
notes: Some definitions include a factor of one half or use 2*dp in the numerator, so check the convention when comparing values. The cavitation number is a related pressure-based dimensionless group.

name: Cauchy Number
description: Computes the dimensionless Cauchy number, the ratio of inertial forces to compressibility (elastic) forces, as density times velocity squared divided by the bulk modulus. High values indicate compressibility effects become significant.
notes: The Cauchy number is the square of the Mach number for an ideal gas, so it links directly to compressible-flow behavior. The bulk modulus must correspond to the fluid's elastic stiffness.

name: Strouhal Number
description: Gives the dimensionless Strouhal number describing oscillating flow, as vortex-shedding frequency times a characteristic length divided by flow velocity. It relates the timescale of unsteady vortex shedding to the flow's convective timescale.
notes: For bluff-body vortex shedding it is often near 0.2 over a wide Reynolds-number range. Use the shedding frequency and the body's cross-stream dimension as the characteristic length.

name: Bond Number
description: Computes the dimensionless Bond number (Eotvos number), the ratio of gravitational (buoyancy) forces to surface-tension forces, as density difference times gravity times length squared divided by surface tension. It indicates whether gravity or capillarity dominates.
notes: Values well below 1 mean surface tension dominates (droplets stay spherical); values above 1 mean gravity flattens the interface. Use the density difference between the two phases, not a single density.

name: Capillary Number
description: Gives the dimensionless capillary number, the ratio of viscous forces to surface-tension forces, as dynamic viscosity times velocity divided by surface tension. It governs the balance between viscous drag and capillarity in multiphase flows.
notes: Low values mean surface tension shapes the interface; high values mean viscous forces deform it. Important in coating, porous-media and microfluidic flows where interfaces are thin.

name: Ohnesorge Number
description: Computes the dimensionless Ohnesorge number, relating viscous forces to inertial and surface-tension forces, as dynamic viscosity divided by the square root of density times surface tension times a characteristic length. It characterizes droplet formation and breakup.
notes: It equals the square root of the Weber number divided by the Reynolds number, independent of velocity. The characteristic length is usually the droplet or jet diameter.

name: Darcy-Weisbach Head Loss
description: Computes the head loss due to pipe friction, as the friction factor times length over diameter times velocity squared divided by two times gravity. The result in meters is the energy loss expressed as an equivalent fluid column height.
notes: This is the head form of the Darcy-Weisbach equation; multiply by density times gravity to get pressure drop. The friction factor depends on Reynolds number and relative roughness.

name: Hagen-Poiseuille Pressure Drop
description: Gives the pressure drop for laminar viscous flow through a circular pipe, as eight times viscosity times length times flow rate divided by pi times radius to the fourth power. The result in pascals is the driving pressure needed to sustain the flow.
notes: The fourth-power dependence on radius makes pressure drop extremely sensitive to pipe diameter. Valid only for steady, laminar, fully developed Newtonian flow; it fails in turbulent regimes.

name: Chezy Velocity
description: Estimates the mean velocity of open-channel flow using the Chezy formula, as the Chezy coefficient times the square root of hydraulic radius times channel slope. The result is in meters per second.
notes: The Chezy coefficient is empirical and depends on channel roughness and geometry; it relates to Manning's n. Assumes steady, uniform flow where the bed slope equals the energy slope.

name: Prandtl Number
description: Computes the dimensionless Prandtl number, the ratio of momentum diffusivity to thermal diffusivity, as dynamic viscosity times specific heat capacity divided by thermal conductivity. It compares how quickly momentum and heat diffuse in a fluid.
notes: It is a fluid property independent of flow geometry; values near 0.7 are typical for gases and much higher for oils. Low values mean heat diffuses faster than momentum, as in liquid metals.

name: Speed of Sound (Ideal Gas)
description: Gives the speed of sound in an ideal gas, as the square root of the heat capacity ratio times the specific gas constant times absolute temperature. The result in meters per second depends only on the gas type and its temperature.
notes: Temperature must be absolute (kelvin), and the specific gas constant is for the particular gas, not the universal constant. Sound speed rises with the square root of temperature and is independent of pressure.

name: Stokes Drag Coefficient
description: Computes the drag coefficient of a sphere in creeping flow, as 24 divided by the Reynolds number. This dimensionless value gives the very high drag coefficients characteristic of slow, viscous-dominated flow around a sphere.
notes: Valid only at low Reynolds number (roughly below 1) where Stokes' law applies. As Reynolds number rises, the true drag coefficient levels off near 0.4 rather than following this inverse relation.

name: Kinematic Viscosity
description: Converts dynamic viscosity to kinematic viscosity by dividing dynamic viscosity by fluid density. The result in square meters per second represents the fluid's momentum diffusivity, the ratio governing how viscous effects spread.
notes: Kinematic viscosity combines viscosity and density into one property used in Reynolds-number calculations. Both inputs should be at the same temperature since each varies with it.

name: Pitot Tube Velocity
description: Recovers flow velocity from a pitot tube's measured dynamic pressure, as the square root of two times dynamic pressure divided by fluid density. The result in meters per second follows from inverting the dynamic-pressure relation.
notes: The pressure must be the dynamic (total minus static) pressure, and it assumes incompressible flow. At high speeds compressibility corrections are needed for accurate results.

name: Buoyant Force
description: Computes the buoyant force on a submerged or floating body by Archimedes' principle, as fluid density times gravity times displaced volume. The result in newtons equals the weight of the fluid displaced and acts upward.
notes: Use the density of the surrounding fluid and the volume it actually displaces, which for a floating body is only the submerged part. The force is independent of the body's own weight or material.

name: Power Number
description: Gives the dimensionless power number of a stirred-tank impeller, as impeller power divided by fluid density times rotational speed cubed times impeller diameter to the fifth power. It characterizes the power draw of mixing impellers.
notes: Rotational speed must be in revolutions per second (consistent with 1/s), and the strong diameter dependence makes units critical. For a given impeller it is roughly constant in the turbulent regime.

name: Fluid Sound Speed (Bulk Modulus)
description: Computes the speed of sound in a liquid or solid, as the square root of the bulk modulus divided by density. The result in meters per second reflects how fast pressure waves propagate through the medium.
notes: Use the adiabatic bulk modulus for acoustic waves. Stiffer (higher bulk modulus) or lighter media transmit sound faster; this form suits nearly incompressible fluids rather than gases.

name: Hydraulic Diameter
description: Computes the hydraulic diameter of a non-circular duct, as four times the flow cross-sectional area divided by the wetted perimeter. The result in meters is an equivalent diameter used in Reynolds-number and friction calculations.
notes: It reduces to the actual diameter for a full circular pipe and equals four times the hydraulic radius. The wetted perimeter counts only the boundary in contact with the fluid.

name: Peclet Number
description: Computes the dimensionless Peclet number for heat transport, the ratio of advection to diffusion, as flow velocity times a characteristic length divided by thermal diffusivity. High values mean advection dominates over conduction.
notes: This thermal Peclet number equals the product of Reynolds and Prandtl numbers; a mass-transfer version uses mass diffusivity instead. Choose the length scale relevant to the transport process.

name: Galilei Number
description: Gives the dimensionless Galilei number, the ratio of gravitational forces to viscous forces, as gravity times a characteristic length cubed divided by kinematic viscosity squared. It appears in problems of buoyancy-driven and film flows.
notes: It is essentially the Grashof number without the temperature-driven density term, and depends strongly on the length scale (cubed). Use kinematic, not dynamic, viscosity here.
